# Manawydan: the stories first, then the spelling

You cannot weigh an accent without knowing what it carries. Here is what **Manawydan** has been carrying.

## The Stories That Carry the Name

**The Seven Who Brought the Head Home.** Manawydan stands beside his brother Brân — Bendigeidfran, the Blessed — when [[matholwch|Matholwch]], king of Ireland, comes to Harlech to ask for their sister Branwen, and he counsels the marriage that begins the whole catastrophe.  When the insult of the mutilated horses has festered into war, Brân wades the sea to Ireland, and the host that crosses with him comes home as seven men: Pryderi, Manawydan, Glifieu Eil Taran, [[taliesin|Taliesin]], Ynawg, Gruddieu fab Muriel, and Heilyn fab Gwyn — bearing the head of Brân, struck by a poisoned spear, which talks with them and is better company than ever it was in life. At Harlech they feast seven years with the head, the three songs of the birds of Rhiannon singing to them, and time does not move.

**The Counsel and the Marriage.** While Brân's host was in Ireland, Caswallawn fab [[beli|Beli]] — Manawydan's own cousin — had struck down the men left in charge and taken the crown of London.  Pryderi, lord of Dyfed and son of Pwyll and [[rhiannon|Rhiannon]], would have fought him; Manawydan counsels otherwise: Caswallawn is their kinsman, and the kingdom has suffered enough of war.  It is the most characteristic speech in the whole Mabinogi — a man with the best claim to vengeance declining it out of arithmetic and mercy.

**The Thunder and the Mist.** They go up Gorsedd Arberth, the mound where, in the First Branch, wonders came to Pwyll — and wonder comes.  As they sit, a peal of thunder falls, and with it a mist so thick they cannot see one another.  When it lifts, Dyfed is gone: no dwelling, no animal, no smoke, no man, no woman — only the four of them and the empty land, house and court and courtiers vanished together.

## The Name Travels

Manawydan's one great comparison is also the deepest fact about him: he is the Welsh form of the figure Ireland knows as [[manannan|Manannán mac Lir]], the sea god and guardian of the Otherworld.  The names are cognates — Ifor Williams derived both from Manaw, the Welsh name of the Isle of Man, so that 'Manawydan' and 'Manannán' each mean, in effect, the Manxman — and the fathers match exactly, Welsh Llŷr against Irish Lir, each a personification of the sea.
